\chapter{A Moment, And Its Two Edges}
\label{ch:el-principio-y-el-fin}
\hlchaptermodality{348}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name el principio, el fin, el instante, la demora and el turno, and say why an ending began as the boundary stone of a field.}

Complete ES-C348-turno: mark where a stretch of time opens and closes, name an instant inside it, report a delay, and claim your turn.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el principio]{el principio — the beginning, and the prince inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C348-principio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the centre}, then \emph{around}. (\emph{El centro}; \emph{alrededor}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item primero · segundo · tercero — the \emph{first} this is built on.
  \item la entrada — the way in, which a beginning resembles.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prin-SI-pio}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft, and \emph{-pio} runs together. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el principio} — \textquotedblleft{}the beginning,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the principle.\textquotedblright{}

Latin built \textbf{princeps} out of two pieces you have already met inside other words: \textbf{prīmus}, \emph{first}, and \textbf{capere}, \emph{to take}. A \emph{princeps} was the one who \textbf{takes first place} — the first name on the senate roll, and later the ruler.

From \emph{princeps} came \textbf{principium}, \emph{the taking of first place}, and so \emph{the start of a thing}.

English keeps both halves of the meaning and spells them differently to tell them apart. A \textbf{principal} is the chief one. A \textbf{principle} is a starting rule, the thing everything else is built on. A \textbf{prince} and a \textbf{principality} are the ruler and the ruled.

Spanish declines to split them: \emph{el principio} is the beginning of a story and the principle of a science with no change of spelling at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first edge of a stretch of time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el principio}
  \item \emph{al principio}
  \item \emph{el principio del día}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words make \emph{princeps}? (\emph{Prīmus}, first, and \emph{capere}, to take.) And which English word means the starting rule of a thing? (Principle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el fin]{el fin — the end, which began as a boundary stone}

\label{lesson:ES-C348-fin}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{around}, then \emph{the beginning}. (\emph{Alrededor}; \emph{el principio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la salida — the way out, which an ending resembles.
  \item primero · segundo · tercero — the order this closes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FIN}, one beat. Short, and the \emph{n} is fully sounded. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el fin} — \textquotedblleft{}the end.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{fīnis} was not a word about time at all. It was a \textbf{boundary} — the stone at the edge of a field, the line where your land stopped and your neighbour's began. A Roman argued about \emph{fines} the way people argue about fences.

Time borrowed the picture afterwards, and now the edge of a stretch of hours is named for the edge of a farm.

English took it in a crowd. Something \textbf{final} is at the boundary. \textbf{Finish} is to reach it. \textbf{Finite} means it has one at all, and \textbf{infinite} means it does not. To \textbf{define} is to set the bounds of a thing; to \textbf{confine} is to hold it inside them; a \textbf{frontier} is a boundary faced outward.

Even \textbf{finance} is here: settling a debt was \emph{finishing} it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both edges of a stretch of time — where it opens and where it stops.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el fin}
  \item \emph{el fin de la semana}
  \item \emph{del principio al fin}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{fīnis} mark? (A boundary, the edge of a field.) And what does \textbf{define} mean, word for word? (To set the bounds of something.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el instante]{el instante — the instant, standing right on top of you}

\label{lesson:ES-C348-instante}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the beginning}, then \emph{the end}. (\emph{El principio}; \emph{el fin}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item estar — the verb this is built on.
  \item la vez — the other way Spanish counts moments.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ins-TAN-te}, three beats with the weight on the second. Spanish keeps both consonants of \emph{-ns-} clearly. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el instante} — \textquotedblleft{}the instant,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the split second.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{īnstāre} is \textbf{in}, \emph{on}, plus \textbf{stāre}, \emph{to stand}: to stand upon something, to press on it, to be right there.

Its present participle was \textbf{īnstāns}, \emph{standing upon} — and that is a remarkably good picture of the present moment. Not the moment that is coming, not the one that has gone: the one with its whole weight on you.

You have that \textbf{stāre} twice already. It is inside \textbf{estar}, the verb for where a thing stands, and inside \textbf{la estación}, a standing-place.

English took the family whole. An \textbf{instant}; an \textbf{instance}, one standing case of a thing; something \textbf{constant}, standing with you; something \textbf{distant}, standing apart; and a \textbf{circumstance}, whatever stands around.

The Spanish phrase to keep is \textbf{en un instante} — in a moment.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two edges and the point between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el instante}
  \item \emph{en un instante}
  \item \emph{un instante, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{īnstāns} mean, word for word? (Standing upon.) And which everyday Spanish verb is the same \emph{stāre}? (\emph{Estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la demora]{la demora — the delay, and the art of hanging back}

\label{lesson:ES-C348-demora}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the end}, then \emph{the instant}. (\emph{El fin}; \emph{el instante}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item temprano — its opposite in a timetable.
  \item la hora — what a delay is measured in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de-MO-ra}, three beats with the weight on the second. One tapped \emph{r}, and the \emph{d} at the front is soft after a vowel. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la demora} — \textquotedblleft{}the delay,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the wait.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mora} was a \emph{lingering}: any stretch of not-yet, whether somebody meant it or not. Add \textbf{dē-} and you get \textbf{demorārī}, to hang about in a place, to be slow leaving.

Notice what the word does not say. It carries no blame. A \emph{demora} is time that passed while nothing happened, and Spanish uses it for a late bus as easily as for a slow reply.

English took two narrow slices. To \textbf{demur} is to hang back from agreeing — the delay moved from the feet to the opinion. A \textbf{moratorium} is an official period of hanging back, a stretch of time in which a thing may not proceed.

Two useful shapes to carry: \textbf{sin demora}, without delay, and \textbf{con demora}, late.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for time that goes by while you wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la demora}
  \item \emph{sin demora}
  \item \emph{hay una demora}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{mora} mean? (A lingering, a pause.) And what does it mean to \textbf{demur}? (To hang back from agreeing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el turno]{el turno — your turn, and the lathe it spins on}

\label{lesson:ES-C348-turno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the instant}, then \emph{the delay}. (\emph{El instante}; \emph{la demora}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la vez — the near neighbour of this word.
  \item otro — whose turn it is next.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TUR-no}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is one tap, and the \emph{u} is a pure \emph{oo}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el turno} — \textquotedblleft{}the turn,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the shift,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}your slot in the queue.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{tórnos} was a tool: the \textbf{lathe}, and also the compass a woodworker used to scribe a circle. Latin borrowed it as \textbf{tornus}, and from there everything round in Europe took its name.

English has a great heap of it. To \textbf{turn}. A \textbf{tour}, which goes round and comes back. A \textbf{tournament}, where riders wheeled at each other. A \textbf{contour}, the line that goes round a shape. \textbf{Return}, \textbf{detour}, \textbf{turnstile} — and \textbf{tornado}, a Spanish word for a wind that turns.

The Spanish sense is the human one. In a bank, in a clinic, on a night shift, people take their \textbf{turno} — the circle comes round and stops at you.

Two shapes worth saying aloud: \textbf{es mi turno}, it's my turn, and \textbf{por turnos}, taking turns.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to cut time up: a beginning, an end, an instant, a delay and a turn.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el turno}
  \item \emph{es mi turno}
  \item \emph{por turnos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tool was a \emph{tórnos}? (A lathe, and a woodworker's compass.) And which storm word is Spanish for a wind that turns? (Tornado.)
\end{tcolorbox}
